explicit_definitions_given: Testimony-confession: acknowledgment of truth with personal commitment and vulnerability
Testimony-narration: telling of a story with content and context
Quasi-judicial trial: witness simultaneously accused and emissary
Hermeneutic appropriation: process by which hearer makes testimony their own

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Addresses the central contradiction (subjective certainty vs objective content) and resolves it through Ricoeur's hermeneutic framework
objections_raised: Apparent contradiction between personal testimony of the Holy Ghost and necessity of historic narrative content

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Philosophical analysis, theological doctrine, scriptural narrative

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Hermeneutic phenomenology (Ricoeur) integrated with LDS theological framework
philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Analytical and synthetic, aiming for integration rather than critique

structural_organization.structure_type: Triangulated funnel: Introduction -> Philosophical framework (Ricoeur) -> Theological framework (LDS) -> Narrative case study (Abinadi) -> Dialectical analysis -> Hermeneutic resolution -> Cosmic expansion -> Conclusion

summary_of_core_decisions: The essay systematically builds a unified theory of testimony by triangulating Ricoeur's semantic/juridical analysis, LDS theology of the Holy Ghost, and the Abinadi narrative. It identifies key dialectical tensions (confession/narration, accused/emissary, subjective/objective) and resolves them through hermeneutic appropriation, ultimately framing testimony as active participation in a cosmic struggle. The argument is well-structured, conceptually precise, and methodologically rigorous, though it relies heavily on Ricoeur's framework and LDS doctrine without critical engagement.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low - the conclusion is assertive and definitive
